title: Connect characters with their story settings
intro: I can explain how a particular place connects with what a character notices, needs or does.
exampleTitle: A place can change a character’s choice
example: Original model: “Ari carried a kite to the oval. A strong wind pulled it sideways. Ari rolled up the string and waited.” The oval and wind are setting clues. Waiting responds to the windy conditions. The text supports that connection; it does not tell us Ari’s age or prove how every windy day ends.
steps: 1. Link a fairytale character and place
Name who and where, then explain a relationship. A setting can make an action possible, difficult or important.

In the Grimm-version Rapunzel premise, the forest tower has a high window but no door or stairs. In Little Red-Cap, the wooded route and flowers affect the child’s journey. Brief original premise cards are in More examples.
How does the tower setting affect an ordinary visit? Compare it with a house that has a door.
Ordinary access is difficult because the tower has no door or stairs. A house with a door offers a different route. This is discussion of story design, not an invitation to climb.
2. Follow a recurring guide on Country
Read the actual named work with an adult. Track a recurring character across two parts and explain how the guide and the particular place connect.

In Cooee Mittigar, written by Jasmine Seymour and illustrated by Leanne Mulgo Watson, Mulgo the black swan guides readers on Darug Country. Prepare the lawful book, glossary and two seasonal spreads using More examples.
What does Mulgo help readers notice on each prepared spread? Point to an actual clue.

Use a word or visible detail from each actual spread and explain its connection with Country or seasonal change. The guide returns across the work. Do not invent a quotation, assume all First Nations stories are the same or treat a summary as the full book.
3. Compare Australian journeys and settings
Creators depict particular places in different ways. Compare what a character sees or does, using evidence from each work.

For Are We There Yet?, Alison Lester’s publisher identifies Grace and her family travelling through the outback, bush and coast. The adult prepares an actual outback spread and a contrasting place before discussing their pictures and words.
Compare one character–place connection in that spread with Mulgo’s guide role. What supports each connection?

Name both works and creators, identify the actual place clues and connect them to the character’s action or role. Accept different supported comparisons. Do not label Darug Country “outback” merely because it is First Nations Country.
mistakes: “Setting is only a place name.”
Conditions and time can also affect a character’s actions.
“All stories from a culture say the same thing.”
Name the specific creators, work and evidence.
“A summary proves I viewed the illustrations.”
Look at the actual supplied spread before making a picture claim.
activity: Use the chart in More examples with a fairytale premise, the prepared Cooee Mittigar spreads and an actual Are We There Yet? outback spread. Add one clue and explain one connection for each. An adult can read or scribe while the child discusses.
adjust: Starter: point to who and where in one short model. Core: connect a setting clue to an action. Stretch: compare two named works and explain an important difference.
safety: Supply the named lawful books and staged pages before their tasks. Respect each creator’s context; do not imitate ceremonies, cultural motifs or risky story actions.
tricky: 1. Does a forest prove a character is frightened?
No. Use actual words, actions or picture clues; a feeling is not guaranteed by a setting.
2. Is every Australian story set in the outback?
No. Use the actual work and its place clues.
3. Can a character change a setting too?
Yes. For example, a story character might plant a garden. Explain the change shown by the text.
faq: Can we begin with the original kite model?
Yes. It teaches the connection method. Follow it with the named authentic literature; it does not replace those works.
Must everyone give the same interpretation?
No. Different ideas can be supported. Explain the actual clue and avoid unsupported certainty.
modelCards: Ari waits instead of flying it

title: Explain which story features you prefer
intro: I can identify a character or setting feature and give a reason for my own preference.
exampleTitle: A preference connects a feature with a response
example: Original story: “Ollie the otter found a lost scarf by the school gate. Ollie put it on the class shelf so its owner could find it.” One reader says, “I like Ollie because returning the scarf is helpful.” Another may prefer an unusual setting. Personal taste can differ; a claim about an action must still fit the text.
steps: 1. Identify a feature before judging it
Characters take part in a story. A setting gives where or when. An event tells what happens. Name the detail you are discussing.
“On the moon, Pip the fox guarded a silver garden. A robot asked for a seed.” Pip and the robot are characters; the moon garden is the setting; asking is an event.
Which supplied detail is a setting? Give a different character detail.
The silver garden on the moon is a setting. Pip is a fox guarding it, and the robot asks for a seed. Keep the feature and its evidence connected.
2. Give a preference and a relevant reason
Say what you prefer, then explain what that feature does for you. A familiar world or an unfamiliar one can each appeal to a reader.

Reader A: “I like the classroom story because helping a new friend feels welcoming.” Reader B: “I prefer the moon garden because I enjoy imagining unusual places.” The complete original stories are in More examples.
Choose one of those settings or characters. Explain your preference using a real detail from the supplied story.
Accept either choice with a connected reason. A child need not share the model reader’s taste or disclose a personal experience. “It is best” alone does not explain the feature.
3. Discuss animal behaviour and different responses
Story animals may act like people. Explain your response to a particular action, keeping it separate from a claim about all real animals.
In the complete Pip story, the fox first hides seeds from the robot, then shares one after noticing an empty pot.
How do you respond to hiding and sharing? Could two readers discuss the same action differently?

For example, a reader may dislike the hiding because it prevents sharing, yet appreciate the later change. Accept another supported response. The fictional fox’s behaviour does not show that every real fox is selfish or kind.
mistakes: “My favourite is the correct favourite.”
Readers can prefer different features for valid reasons.
“Retelling is the whole response.”
Add how a feature affects your preference.
“One action describes every animal.”
Discuss this fictional character and this action.
activity: Read both complete stories and response cards in More examples. Name the feature each reader values. Make your own preference response with one detail, then listen to a different supported choice.
adjust: Starter: choose a feature from the supplied cards. Core: connect a preference and a reason. Stretch: explain why two different responses can both make sense.
safety: An adult may read the stories aloud or scribe a response. Judge the feature–reason connection, not agreement with the adult, handwriting or private experiences.
tricky: 1. Can I prefer an unfamiliar world?
Yes. Explain which actual feature interests you and why.
2. Can I dislike a character’s action but enjoy the story?
Yes. A troubling action can create interest or help a character change.
3. Does “I like it because it is good” give much evidence?
No. Name a feature and explain its effect on you.
faq: Must I use the word because?
It is a useful starter, but another clear way of giving a reason is valid.
Can a picture be the feature I prefer?
Yes, when you can point to the actual supplied illustration and explain your response.
modelCaption: Name the feature; explain your response

title: Explain how story words create an impression
intro: I can compare words that help readers imagine characters and settings.
exampleTitle: Changing a verb changes the impression
example: Original versions: “Mara walked down the hall” and “Mara stomped down the hall.” Stomped suggests forceful steps and may suggest anger or frustration. Walked gives less detail about the movement. Neither sentence proves what Mara always feels. Compare actual language, then explain a supported impression.
steps: 1. Compare actions and dialogue
Look at verbs, whole verb groups and speech as well as adjectives. Explain how a word helps present the character in that moment.
“Rae was carrying the bags. ‘You can rest,’ Rae whispered.” Compare “Rae was dragging the bags. ‘Hurry up!’ Rae snapped.”
Name one language change and explain a possible effect.

Was carrying / was dragging changes the action; whispered / snapped changes how speech is presented. The offer of rest can suggest care, while the sharp command can suggest impatience. Other interpretations need the actual words, not a permanent label for Rae.
2. Compare setting and seasonal clues
Read a whole description before selecting words. Sounds, light, plants and weather can shape a reader’s picture.
Version A: “Soft rain tapped the window. New leaves shone.” Version B: “Hard rain hammered the window. Bare branches shook.”
How do tapped and hammered change the impression? Can you name a season with certainty?

Tapped can suggest gentler rain; hammered suggests a stronger sound or force. The plant clues may suggest seasonal change, but these short invented scenes do not establish a named season for every place in Australia.
3. Read landscape language in a specific First Nations text
Use the actual creator’s words and their context. A glossary can help explain an unfamiliar word; do not invent its meaning from a picture alone.
Adult prepares two actual landscape descriptions in Cooee Mittigar by Jasmine Seymour and Leanne Mulgo Watson. Keep the lawful book open, with the glossary and source preparation in More examples.
Point to a word in each prepared description. What picture or relationship does that wording help you understand?

Name the real word and explain a supported effect using the page and glossary. Nura refers to Country in this Darug source, including relationships and belonging. Do not substitute a generic invented “Aboriginal landscape quote” or assume the word is local everywhere.
mistakes: “Only adjectives matter.”
Actions, dialogue and verb groups shape meaning too.
“A possible feeling is a certain fact.”
Explain the clue and qualify an inference where needed.
“Different words always mean the same thing.”
Compare the impression created in the complete context.
activityTitle: Change one word and explain the effect
activity: Use the complete paired passages in More examples. Highlight an action or setting word, replace it to make a new fictional version, then explain the changed impression. Compare this with one real phrase in the prepared literary book.
adjust: Starter: compare walked and stomped. Core: explain a word–impression link in two passages. Stretch: compare a whole verb group or a specific landscape phrase without making a universal claim.
safety: An adult may read the passages and accept speech, pointing, AAC or a scribed explanation. Attribute actual cultural language and avoid reproducing or imitating cultural artwork.
tricky: 1. Does stomped prove Mara is always angry?
No. It suggests a way of moving and a possible feeling in this moment.
2. Can the same place be described as peaceful or lonely?
Yes. Different details can create different impressions; show the actual words.
3. Is a rewritten line still the author’s original wording?
No. Clearly call it your changed fictional version.
faq: Do I need to learn difficult analysis labels?
Begin with the actual word, what it describes and its effect. Use useful terms after an example.
Can two readers give different impressions?
Yes, if they can explain real language clues and keep unsupported guesses separate.
modelCaption: Compare language, then explain its effect

title: Hear, reproduce and change word patterns
intro: I can notice a spoken pattern, reproduce it and explain a change I make.
exampleTitle: A steady pulse can hold different word rhythms
example: Original chant: “Tap, tap, little rain. / Tap, tap, come again.” The repeated opening helps listeners join in. An adult says it naturally, then models the separate four-pulse example below. A pulse is evenly spaced time; word rhythm is how sounds and silences fit within it. You need to perform or use an agreed accessible equivalent, not only name the pattern.
steps: 1. Notice sounds in a complete rhyme
Say the whole rhyme and listen for matching endings or repeated words. Rhyme depends on pronunciation, not just final letters.
Original lines: “Little boat beside the shore, / Gentle waves come back once more.” Shore and more have matching spoken endings in the model.
Name the rhyme pair. Is repeating the same opening a different kind of pattern?
Shore / more is the rhyme pair. Repeating an opening such as “Tap, tap” is word repetition. A rhyme need not use identical spelling, and not every poem needs a rhyme.
2. Reproduce a rhythm against a pulse
Keep four equal spans at a comfortable pace. A rest is silent time; two short sounds can share one span. The adult models the supplied pattern before the learner echoes it.
Use the actual table below: TAP | REST | TAP + TAP | HUM. The plus sign means two short sounds inside one pulse span.
Echo the pattern, including the silent span. How many pulse spans and how many sounded events are there?

There are four pulse spans and four sounded events: one tap, two taps and one hum. They are distributed differently across time. Observe the real timing and silence; a correct written count alone does not demonstrate reproduction.
3. Experiment and compare
Keep one feature recognisable while changing another. Compare a permitted home-language rhyme using an actual family or community model, with its meaning explained.
Change the final HUM in the four-span model to the spoken word SUN while keeping its span. Then try two quick hums in that span and compare the rhythm.
Which change keeps one sounded event in the last span, and which subdivides that span?

One SUN replaces humming with a spoken word while keeping one event in the modelled span. Two quick hums subdivide the span and change the rhythm. Actual pronunciation may affect syllables, so model the intended version. Do not call a louder performance alone a new rhythm.
mistakes: “Beat and word rhythm are always identical.”
A steady pulse can contain silence or several short sounds.
“Rhyme is matching letters.”
Say the words and compare spoken endings.
“Reading a plan proves performance.”
Observe the actual reproduced pattern and note support.
activity: Use the whole rhyme and pulse model in More examples. Echo it, make one deliberate change and explain what stayed recognisable. With a willing adult or family member, compare one repeated sound or word in a known permitted home-language rhyme.
adjust: Starter: echo two words with adult modelling. Core: reproduce the four spans with a rest. Stretch: alter one subdivision and explain how its timing changes.
safety: Accept comfortable voice, pace and accessible ways to represent timing. Do not grade accent or require personal cultural performance. Home-language models need a real knowledgeable source; do not invent translations.
tricky: 1. Do four pulses always mean four syllables?
No. One pulse can be silent or contain more than one syllable.
2. Is a louder repeat necessarily a different rhythm?
No. Loudness can change while timing remains the same.
3. Must again rhyme with rain for every speaker?
No. Pronunciation varies; do not mark an accent wrong.
faq: Can I tap rather than clap?
Yes, or agree an accessible equivalent. State which timing or word pattern you are observing.
Must every home language use the same rhyme pattern?
No. Compare actual examples and their meanings without assuming all languages work alike.
modelCaption: Pulse is steady; words can vary inside it
modelCards: Two short sounds in one span

title: Adapt a story and edit your new version
intro: I can keep a recognisable story pattern, make meaningful changes and improve my own creation.
exampleTitle: Keep a pattern while changing the story
example: Original story: “Nell carried a seed to the garden. Rain began. Nell waited under a shelter. When the rain stopped, Nell planted the seed.” A new version can give a robot a seed-delivery goal, a wheel stuck in moon dust and help from a friend. Goal, difficulty, response and ending remain recognisable, while the characters and events change.
steps: 1. Notice a structure you can adapt
Read or hear the whole familiar model first. Map the connected events before deciding what to keep and change. Not every literary text needs a problem–solution pattern.
In the supplied Nell story, the planting goal meets rain, Nell waits, and planting follows after the rain stops.
If your version is on the moon with a robot, what should remain connected?

The robot needs a clear goal, a fitting difficulty or sequence and an ending that follows its response. Changing a name alone gives little new story meaning. Other literary structures can be adapted when they are the chosen model.
2. Change language and mode deliberately
Invent dialogue, behaviour or description that suits the new version. Drawing, writing, performance or an adult-approved digital tool can tell connected events.
Original model: “The robot called.” New fictional detail: “The robot with a long silver arm called from the garden gate.” The extra phrases describe which robot and where it calls.
Create a new line of speech for the stuck robot and a drawing or caption that fits it.

Accept a coherent original line such as asking a friend for help, with a fitting visual or performance. Label added details as invented. A spoken line, drawing or digital panel should tell story meaning rather than merely name a tool.
3. Edit meaning, then reread
Check event order, clear references, useful detail and whether the ending fits. Editing includes more than spelling and neatness.
Out-of-order draft: “Nell planted the seed. The rain stopped. Nell waited under a shelter.” The complete original and changed story are in More examples.
Move the events into a coherent order, then make one visible edit in your own version.

For the model: Nell waits, the rain stops, then Nell plants. In the learner’s story, inspect the actual revision and ask why it helps. Accept another coherent sequence when its different meaning is explained.
mistakes: “Adapting means copying everything.”
Keep an identifiable pattern and make meaningful original choices.
“An ending can ignore the earlier events.”
Check that the new ending follows the established story.
“Editing only fixes spelling.”
Improve sequence, clarity, dialogue or detail too.
activityTitle: Make four panels, then revise one
activity: Use the complete familiarised Nell story in More examples. Plan a changed character, setting and event across four panels. Tell or write the story, revise one part and show how it improves the meaning.
adjust: Starter: adult models the event map. Core: make a coherent changed version. Stretch: adapt dialogue and description across two modes, keeping events consistent.
safety: Observe the actual creation and edit, with support recorded. Use original drawings and safe performance; do not imitate culturally restricted stories, ceremonies or artwork.
tricky: 1. Is changing only the title a rich adaptation?
Usually not. Show how a character, event, language choice or telling method changes meaning.
2. Can a drawing carry an event?
Yes. Explain what it shows and how it connects to the next part.
3. Can two different endings both work?
Yes, when each fits the established events and intended new meaning.
faq: Must I use a digital tool?

No device is compulsory for every learner. More examples also offers a concrete adult-supported digital task: create two original story screens, order them, revise a caption and reread the changed version.
Can an adult help write my words?
Yes. Record the support and keep the learner’s own story choices and explanation visible.
modelCards: Change: robot stuck in moon dust

title: Compare how texts present the same topic
intro: I can find shared information and explain how different texts organise or show it.
exampleTitle: Same topic does not mean the same information
example: Original pair: “A tadpole wriggled past Tilly’s boot. Later Tilly noticed small legs.” Information card: “Tadpoles hatch from frog eggs. As they develop, legs grow and their bodies change.” Both mention tadpoles and legs. The story follows a character’s noticing; the information groups facts and includes eggs, which the story does not mention.
steps: 1. Compare a poem, narrative and information
Begin with the shared topic. Read each complete text, then identify the information it actually supplies and how it presents it.
The three original frog-growth texts in More examples use a poem’s lines and sound pattern, Tilly’s events, and an information card’s stage facts.
What shared topic links them? Does every text name all the life stages?

Frog growth links them. No: the information card names eggs, tadpoles, froglets and adults; the poem and narrative select fewer details. A title or text-type label alone does not supply missing facts.
2. Sort shared and unique details
Compare one detail at a time. A detail is shared only when each chosen text supplies it. Separate prior knowledge from what the texts state.
In the worked pair above, both mention tadpoles and legs; only the information card mentions eggs. Only the story names Tilly.
Where would Tilly and eggs go in a both / story only / information only chart? Explain.
Tilly belongs under story only; eggs under information only. Neither belongs under both. Their placement depends on these actual supplied texts, not a rule about what every story or report contains.
3. Compare recipe formats
A packet panel, book page, video or digital card can share a making purpose. Their features can help readers follow ingredients, order or movement in different ways.
More examples supplies three original fruit-bowl recipe layouts. An adult can open the named ABC Annaka vegetable-truck recipe video and compare an actual making section.
What stays similar across the recipes, and what could the actual video add to the static versions?

Ingredients and ordered actions support making something. A viewed video can show movement over time and provide spoken explanation. Use an actual observed detail after viewing; if only a transcript was read, do not claim video observation. Different recipes need not have identical ingredients.
mistakes: “Same topic means identical facts.”
Check each actual detail before calling it shared.
“Every story has headings like a report.”
Compare the organisation that is really present.
“A description of a video means I watched it.”
Distinguish reading a transcript from viewing movement.
activity: Use the complete frog texts in More examples. Record one shared detail, one detail only in a selected text and one presentation difference. Compare the prepared recipe formats and explain which feature helps a reader follow steps.
adjust: Starter: compare two short cards with an adult. Core: classify supplied information and organisation. Stretch: choose a format for a particular reading need and justify it.
safety: An adult may read text aloud. This is a reading comparison: no cooking or food handling is needed. Use the named video with adult guidance only when its viewing is part of the comparison.
tricky: 1. Does a poem have to include every fact about its topic?
No. It can select details for its particular purpose.
2. Can a digital recipe look like a printed one?
Yes. Screen delivery does not guarantee animation or different wording.
3. Can a story contain a true fact?
Yes. Decide from the complete text, not a rigid fiction-versus-fact shortcut.
faq: Must both texts have the same title?
No. Use their actual topic and information.
Can a picture or diagram change the presentation?
Yes. Inspect the real labels, arrows or image information and explain what they add.
modelCaption: Share a topic; select and organise differently

title: Listen, respond and build ideas together
intro: I can show understanding, add a connected idea and give or follow clear instructions.
exampleTitle: A connected reply shows what was understood
example: Original exchange: “The reading corner needs a lamp so we can see the books.” Reply: “You think a lamp would help us see. Where could we put it?” The reply restates the idea and asks about a missing detail. Listening is shown by the relevant response, not a compulsory gaze or posture.
steps: 1. Listen, restate and clarify
Attend in a way that works for you. Say the main idea back without changing it, then ask a useful question about something unclear.
Speaker: “Let’s put the seed pots by the window because they need light.” Reply: “You want the pots near the window for light.”
Ask one relevant question that could help carry out the idea.
For example, ask which window, how many pots or where on the sill they should go. A useful question connects to the actual contribution. Do not insist on one memorised phrase.
2. Extend ideas and respond respectfully
A statement can add information; an opinion gives a view. You may agree or disagree while keeping your response relevant and respectful.
“I prefer a quiet reading game because I can hear the story.” Another speaker says, “I have a different thought: a word hunt would let us look for clues.”
Offer one connected reason or suggestion, then invite the other person’s view.

Accept different preferences with relevant reasons and respectful language. A suggestion should add useful detail, such as taking turns choosing games. Merely changing the topic does not extend the earlier idea.
3. Give, receive and repair instructions
State the goal and the steps in a usable order. Check the listener’s response and clarify missing objects or positions.
Paper task: draw a square; put a small circle inside it; draw a star above the square. No scissors are needed.
Give or follow those directions with a partner. How would you repair “Put it there”?

Name the object and position, for example “Put the small circle inside the square.” Compare the actual drawing with the directions, then swap roles. Naming good listening alone does not demonstrate taking part in the exchange.
mistakes: “Listening means waiting to speak.”
Show understanding of the other person’s main idea.
“Disagreement must be rude.”
Offer a respectful alternative and a relevant reason.
“A clear instruction needs no checking.”
Check what the listener understood and repair uncertainty.
activity: Use the complete idea, opinion and paper-direction cards in More examples. Restate a partner’s idea, give one connected response, follow directions and then lead them. Discuss one repair that helped.
adjust: Starter: adult models a restatement or question. Core: contribute relevantly and follow three directions. Stretch: combine two ideas or revise an instruction after a misunderstanding.
safety: Accept spoken language, AAC and suitable access support; record prompts. Do not grade eye contact, accent or a fixed posture. Judge the meaning and usefulness of actual contributions.
tricky: 1. Must I agree to show I listened?
No. An accurate restatement and relevant respectful alternative can show understanding.
2. Is “I like the way you…” always useful?
It needs a real, specific completion connected to the contribution.
3. Can a question improve an instruction?
Yes. Ask about a missing object, position, step or goal.
faq: What if I did not hear part of the message?
Ask for repetition or clarification; adjust the communication conditions where useful.
Can an adult act as the partner?
Yes. Preserve the learner’s own contribution and note the support used.
modelCaption: Understand first; then add something useful

title: Find a text’s purpose and audience
intro: I can explain what a text aims to do and who its choices address.
exampleTitle: Topic, purpose and audience ask different questions
example: Original advertisement: “Families, join our Saturday library story club. Share a story together and discover a new favourite book!” Topic: a library story club. Main purpose: encourage participation. Intended audience clue: Families. Other people can read it too; the named audience is not a ban on other readers.
steps: 1. Find what the text aims to do
Read the whole text. Imaginative texts can entertain or explore ideas; informative texts give information; persuasive texts try to influence a reader. A text can have more than one purpose.
Compare: “The books whispered to the moon boat”; “The library opens at nine”; “Join our Saturday story club!”
Which asks the reader to take action? Which gives an opening-time fact?

Join our Saturday story club encourages action. The library opening sentence informs. The moon-boat line imagines an event. Use these actual clues, rather than a rule that a certain picture or format proves a purpose.
2. Identify intended readers from clues
Look at direct address, information needed, wording and context. A sign, advertisement or poster can have different purposes.
Sign: “Library visitors: return borrowed books in this box.” Advertisement: “Families, join our Saturday library story club.”
Who does each address, and what does it ask them to do?

The sign addresses library visitors returning books; the advertisement addresses families and encourages joining the club. These are intended-reader clues, not claims that nobody else can read the messages.
3. Discuss a named First Nations author’s purpose
Use the actual work and its specific creator. Do not assume all books by a group of authors have one purpose.
Prepare Jasmine Seymour’s Open Your Heart to Country using the lawful book or authorised ABC author reading named in More examples. The work invites reconnection with Country, family and language.
Which actual clue supports an invitation or connection purpose? Can it also help readers learn?

Point to a real part of the supplied work and explain the purpose it supports. More than one purpose may be justified. The brief description here is not the full book, and no ceremony or personal family disclosure is required.
mistakes: “Purpose is the same as topic.”
Topic is what it is about; purpose is what it aims to do.
“Every poster persuades.”
A poster may inform, direct, invite or persuade; inspect the actual text.
“Audience means everyone else is excluded.”
Intended readers are suggested by choices; others may still read it.
activityTitle: Give a purpose, audience and clue
activity: Sort the complete texts, sign and advertisement in More examples. Explain one purpose and intended audience with a real clue. With the prepared named literary work, discuss another supported purpose.
adjust: Starter: choose between an imagined event and a stated fact. Core: connect purpose and audience with evidence. Stretch: explain two purposes in one text or rewrite an original message for a different reader.
safety: An adult can read and prepare the actual source. Attribute First Nations creators and Country correctly; do not infer cultural meaning from identity alone or imitate restricted cultural practices.
tricky: 1. Does a photograph prove a text is informative?
No. Advertisements, stories and informative texts can all use photographs.
2. Can an invitation inform and persuade?
Yes. It may give event facts while encouraging attendance.
3. Is every First Nations text written for the same audience?
No. Examine the specific work and its choices.
faq: Must a text have only one purpose?
No. Explain its main purpose or supported combination.
Can a sign be helpful without an image?
Yes. Its actual words and context may clearly identify readers and an action.

title: Read accurately, phrase naturally and repair meaning
intro: I can read the printed words, group ideas and reread to check or correct them.
exampleTitle: Check print before accepting a word
example: Printed sentence: “The children planted six seeds.” If it is read as “six seats”, stop and inspect the final letters and sounds. Seeds has d before its final s; seats has t. Read the actual printed word, then reread the whole sentence to check its meaning. A sensible guess alone is not enough.
steps: 1. Use sound, word and meaningful-part knowledge
Check the full printed word. Blend known sound–letter patterns, recognise learnt words and use helpful bases, endings or compounds. Then check the sentence meaning.
Planted contains plant + ed; lunchbox contains lunch + box. In this word, the ending ed helps show a past action.
Read planted and lunchbox, then say how a useful part helped.

Listen to the actual reading and explanation. Plant plus the past ending supports planted; lunch and box form lunchbox. Do not model the assessed target aloud immediately before an independent reading attempt. Not every word is fully predictable from one simple pattern.
2. Read phrases for connected meaning
Group words in useful units and use punctuation to guide the voice. Fluency includes accuracy, natural phrasing and understanding, not racing.
“After lunch, the children carried a seed box to the garden.” One model groups After lunch / the children carried a seed box / to the garden.
Read the full passage in More examples. Try a natural phrase grouping, then reread smoothly.

Accept sensible alternative groupings that keep meaning and do not split words mechanically. Listen for accurate words and useful pauses; do not demand an identical accent, voice or fixed reading speed. Record adult modelling separately from independent reading.
3. Monitor and self-correct
Notice when print, grammar or meaning does not fit. Go back, inspect the word and reread the connected sentence after a repair.
Controlled adult slip: the child sees “The children planted six seeds” while the adult says “The children planted six seats.” The actual passage is supplied in More examples.
Which printed word needs checking? Repair it and reread. During your own reading, notice a mismatch if one occurs.

Seeds is printed, not seats. Check the letters and say the corrected sentence. A controlled detection task practises repair; record spontaneous self-correction separately. Do not create a fake learner mistake or treat a selection answer as fluent reading.
mistakes: “Fastest means most fluent.”
Accuracy, meaningful phrasing and understanding matter.
“A picture can tell me which printed word to guess.”
Decode the print; use meaning to check the result.
“Rereading is a failure.”
Rereading can restore meaning and build confidence.
activity: Use the actual passage and word cards in More examples. Read once, discuss one meaning question, then reread with useful phrasing. An adult records support, accurate word reading and any actual self-correction.
adjust: Starter: model a different short line before guided reading. Core: read the supplied connected passage. Stretch: transfer to another suitable decodable text and explain a real repair.
safety: Give directions aloud if needed while keeping assessed text for the learner to read. Use appropriate access accommodations and note what competence was observed. A paper score cannot certify oral fluency.
tricky: 1. Is one pause pattern compulsory?
No. Accept a natural grouping that preserves the sentence’s meaning.
2. Does context replace checking the letters?
No. A plausible word can still be different from the word printed.
3. Is a prompted repair independent self-correction?
No. Record the prompt and distinguish it from a spontaneous repair.
faq: Can we reread a familiar passage?
Yes. Also try a different suitable passage when checking transfer; do not confuse memorisation with new word reading.
Should every frequent word be memorised as irregular?
No. Use its actual sound–letter and word-part patterns, and teach any unusual part explicitly.

title: Use clues to understand, infer and check
intro: I can use reading strategies to explain stated and inferred meaning, then check it against evidence.
exampleTitle: A prediction can change after a new clue
example: Original text: “Nell reached the garden with a seed envelope. Rain began, so Nell waited under a shelter.” A supported prediction is that she may wait for the rain to stop before planting. It is a possibility, not a fact already stated. The next line, “When the rain stopped, Nell planted the seeds,” confirms this particular prediction.
steps: 1. Visualise, predict and connect
Imagine the stated scene, use relevant knowledge and predict from clues. Keep invented details separate from what the text actually says. Check predictions as you read.
Title: Seeds for the garden. Before reading, possible topic words include garden or seed. The complete station-and-garden story is in More examples.
After reading, which predicted words actually occur? Name one stated detail and one imagined detail that is not supplied.

Check the real passage. Garden and seed-related words occur; other predictions may not. Nell’s rain shelter is stated, but a chosen coat colour is not. A relevant connection can help explain meaning without making it a new text fact.
2. Combine print, an image and prior knowledge
Literal meaning is directly stated. An inference links actual clues with relevant knowledge. Check that it fits and acknowledge what remains unknown.
Words: “The child filled the tray.” Inspect the actual illustration below before making a picture claim.
What does the picture add? What supports the idea of a bird feeder, and what can you not know yet?

It shows seeds pouring into a hanging tray and a bird nearby. These clues support the feeder inference. They do not prove the bird’s next action or species. The text does not give the child’s name. Accept other supported observations; keep an invented next event labelled as a prediction.
3. Summarise, question and repair understanding
Keep the main idea and important connected events. Ask a useful question about missing information; reread when a proposed meaning conflicts with the text.
The organiser below gives the shorter seed story’s order. The complete longer story, a fact card and listening directions are in More examples.
Give a short summary. What is wrong with “Nell planted before the rain stopped”? Ask one useful unanswered question.

Nell brings seeds, waits through rain and plants after it stops. The proposed order conflicts with the actual ending. A question such as what grew later is unanswered by this story. Accept another relevant question; do not invent its answer as a stated fact.
mistakes: “An inference is any guess.”
Link a real clue and useful knowledge, then check consistency.
“A summary repeats every detail.”
Keep the main idea and essential connected events.
“A mental picture is all in the text.”
Distinguish actual details from what you imagined.
activity: Use the complete story in More examples. Predict likely topic words, visualise a scene, connect one relevant idea and check a prediction. Summarise the events with an organiser, then ask a useful question. Listen to the actual fact card and directions and check the stated details.
adjust: Starter: adult reads and models a clue–idea link. Core: explain a supported inference and short summary. Stretch: revise an inference after a new clue or explain why an unanswered question remains open.
safety: An adult may read when comprehension is the target and accept speech, drawing, AAC or writing. Record support. The feeder picture is for interpreting evidence; it does not require feeding wildlife or taking a real train trip.
tricky: 1. Can two predictions both be reasonable?
Yes, if both fit the clues. Later text may confirm one, reject one or leave both open.
2. Does the fact card’s four shoots mean the other seeds can never grow?
No. It records what was visible on the stated day.
3. Can an organiser help with information as well as stories?
Yes. Labels, groups or sequence arrows can show the main information and its relationships.
faq: Must I use every strategy on every sentence?
No. Choose a strategy for the reading need and explain how it helps.
What if my personal connection differs from another reader’s?
That is fine. Keep the link relevant and check any claim about the text against its evidence.
